editorialNote: This resource helps readers find the right kind of help. Contributor types are identified honestly; biographical facts and publications are sourced, while strengths, limitations, and comparisons are labeled HomeGroups assessments.

scholars.name: Craig S. Keener
scholars.title: F. M. and Ada Thompson Professor of Biblical Studies, Asbury Theological Seminary
scholars.tradition: Christian New Testament scholarship; Pentecostal and evangelical contexts
scholars.overview: A New Testament scholar especially known for placing the Gospels and Acts within their early Jewish and Greco-Roman environments.
languages: The reviewed public biography does not provide a complete self-reported language inventory. His technical work requires sustained engagement with Koine Greek and translated ancient Jewish and Greco-Roman sources, but this profile does not convert that professional use into unsupported fluency claims.
strengths: Exceptional breadth of ancient comparative material
Combines large technical commentaries with accessible teaching
Particularly useful for social, rhetorical, Jewish, and Greco-Roman context
Engages historical questions without concealing his Christian commitments
limitations: The enormous quantity of parallels can require readers to distinguish close contextual evidence from looser analogy.
His historical and theological judgments are often more confident than those of strongly skeptical historical critics.
His work is strongest in New Testament context; Hebrew Bible textual criticism is not his principal specialization.
writings: The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament
The Gospel of John: A Commentary
The Historical Jesus of the Gospels
Miracles: The Credibility of the New Testament Accounts
The Gospel of Matthew: A Socio-Rhetorical Commentary
contributions: Made a very large body of ancient background material available to pastors and nonspecialists
Produced one of the most extensively documented modern commentaries on Acts
Brought global Christian testimony and miracle claims into sustained historical discussion
Helped popularize contextual rather than isolated readings of New Testament passages
scholars.influence: Highly influential in evangelical and Pentecostal biblical studies, pastoral training, Bible-background resources, and historically oriented defenses of New Testament reliability.
comparisons: With Richard Bauckham: both treat the Gospels as historically serious sources. Bauckham emphasizes named testimony and eyewitness transmission; Keener more often emphasizes broad social-historical and literary context.

With Emanuel Tov: Keener normally begins from the received critical editions used in New Testament study, whereas Tov's specialty is the prior textual plurality and transmission history of Hebrew Scripture.

With James Kugel and Jon Levenson: Keener makes extensive use of Jewish sources for New Testament context, while Kugel and Levenson center Jewish interpretation and the Hebrew Bible on their own terms.
scholars.who: A New Testament scholar who specializes in explaining the Jewish, Greco-Roman, cultural, and historical world behind the Gospels and Acts.
scholars.whyHelpful: Keener can help ordinary readers see why a passage made sense to its first audience. His background work is especially useful when modern assumptions make a New Testament scene, custom, argument, or miracle account difficult to understand.

startWith.title: The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament
startWith.reason: The most accessible place to look up the cultural background of a particular passage.

startWith.title: The Historical Jesus of the Gospels
startWith.reason: A fuller introduction to how he evaluates Yeshua historically.

scholars.name: James L. Kugel
scholars.title: Professor Emeritus of Bible, Bar-Ilan University; former Starr Professor of Hebrew Literature, Harvard University
scholars.overview: A scholar of the Hebrew Bible, Dead Sea Scrolls, and the history of biblical interpretation, especially the assumptions through which ancient interpreters read Scripture.
languages: His scholarship works directly with Biblical Hebrew and ancient Jewish texts. His public biography and bibliography demonstrate substantial Hebrew-language scholarship, but the reviewed biography does not present a complete self-rated language inventory.
strengths: Explains ancient interpretation with unusual clarity
Shows how later readers shaped the Bible's received meaning
Moves effectively between literary criticism, Second Temple interpretation, and Jewish theology
Writes for both specialists and general readers
limitations: His distinction between the Bible's earlier meanings and later interpretive Bible can unsettle readers who assume a single continuous meaning.
Some historical reconstructions depend upon dating and source-critical judgments that remain debated.
His readable syntheses can compress disagreements that require fuller specialist treatment.
contributions: Clarified the shared assumptions of ancient Jewish and Christian biblical interpreters
Helped distinguish the compositional world of biblical texts from their early reception
Made the history of interpretation central to understanding what later communities call the Bible
Connected Dead Sea Scrolls and rewritten Scripture to broader interpretive history
scholars.influence: Influential across Hebrew Bible, reception history, early Judaism, literary study, and public conversations about historical criticism and traditional faith.
comparisons: With Jon Levenson: both read the Hebrew Bible within Jewish interpretive history. Kugel foregrounds the rise of ancient interpretation; Levenson more often develops literary and theological meaning across Jewish tradition.
With Emanuel Tov: Kugel concentrates on how texts were interpreted, while Tov concentrates on the manuscripts and textual forms being interpreted.
With Craig Keener and Richard Bauckham: Kugel is generally less focused on defending New Testament historical claims and more focused on the changing interpretive life of Israel's Scriptures.

sources.label: James Kugel official biography and CV

scholars.who: A Jewish scholar of the Hebrew Bible and the history of how ancient Jews and Christians interpreted it.
scholars.whyHelpful: Kugel helps readers notice the difference between what a biblical passage may have meant in its earliest setting and what generations of interpreters later understood it to mean. He is especially helpful when a familiar interpretation seems obvious but is not stated directly in the passage.

startWith.title: How to Read the Bible
startWith.reason: His broadest and most readable guide to the tension between modern biblical scholarship and traditional reading.

startWith.title: The Bible As It Was
startWith.reason: A focused introduction to how ancient interpreters understood biblical stories.

scholars.name: Emanuel Tov
scholars.title: J. L. Magnes Professor of Bible Emeritus, Hebrew University of Jerusalem
scholars.overview: A leading specialist in the textual criticism of the Hebrew Bible, Septuagint, and Dead Sea Scrolls, and former editor-in-chief of the international Dead Sea Scrolls Publication Project.
expertise: Textual criticism of the Hebrew Bible
languages: Hebrew and Greek are directly reflected in his education and primary research: his BA included Bible and Greek literature, and his doctorate examined the Septuagint translation of Jeremiah. His work also engages Aramaic and other textual languages, but this profile avoids assigning conversational fluency without a self-reported inventory.
strengths: Exceptional control of manuscript evidence and scribal phenomena
Careful classification of textual variants without forcing them into one simple history
Combines theory, editions, and large collaborative publication projects
Provides essential safeguards against arguments built on an assumed single ancient text form
limitations: Textual criticism can identify forms and relationships without by itself resolving theological meaning.
His technical work can be difficult for nonspecialists.
Proposed textual relationships and categories remain open to revision as manuscripts and methods are reassessed.
writings: Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible
The Text-Critical Use of the Septuagint in Biblical Research
Scribal Practices and Approaches Reflected in the Texts Found in the Judean Desert
The Dead Sea Scrolls Reader, co-edited
contributions: Directed the Dead Sea Scrolls publication project through the release of dozens of Discoveries in the Judaean Desert volumes
Established widely used methods for evaluating Hebrew Bible textual witnesses
Advanced the study of textual plurality in the Second Temple period
Helped create print and electronic research editions of Hebrew, Greek, and Judean Desert texts
scholars.influence: Foundational for contemporary Hebrew Bible textual criticism, Septuagint studies, Dead Sea Scrolls research, Bible translation, and critical editions.
comparisons: With James Kugel: Tov asks which textual form a community possessed; Kugel asks how communities interpreted Scripture. The questions are complementary but not interchangeable.
With Jon Levenson: Tov's method is primarily philological and text-critical; Levenson's is more literary and theological.
With Keener and Bauckham: Tov's work cautions all historical and theological interpreters to identify the textual witness behind a quotation before building an argument upon its wording.

sources.label: Hebrew University Department of Bible profile

scholars.who: A leading textual scholar who studies the ancient manuscripts behind modern editions and translations of the Hebrew Bible.
scholars.whyHelpful: Tov helps readers ask a question that comes before interpretation: Which ancient wording are we interpreting? His work explains why the Masoretic Text, Septuagint, Samaritan Pentateuch, and Dead Sea Scrolls sometimes preserve different forms of a passage.

startWith.title: Introductory lectures and interviews on Hebrew Bible textual history
startWith.reason: The best first step for a general reader before entering his technical books.

startWith.title: Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible
startWith.reason: The standard full study when you are ready for technical detail.

helpfulFor: How the Hebrew Bible was transmitted

scholars.name: Richard Bauckham
scholars.title: Biblical scholar and theologian; former Professor of New Testament Studies, University of St Andrews
scholars.overview: A New Testament scholar and theologian known especially for work on Gospel eyewitness testimony, early Christology, Revelation, Jewish and Christian apocalyptic literature, and the early Jerusalem church.
languages: The reviewed official biography does not publish a complete language inventory. His technical work engages New Testament Greek and ancient Jewish and Christian texts; this profile does not infer a full list or level of fluency.
strengths: Connects detailed textual observations with large historical arguments
Brings neglected names, traditions, and early Jewish sources into Gospel research
Works across New Testament, early Judaism, theology, and ecological interpretation
Produces both specialist monographs and accessible books
limitations: The eyewitness model advanced in Jesus and the Eyewitnesses remains substantially debated.
Some arguments build broad historical conclusions from patterns of names, testimony, and literary detail that other scholars weigh differently.
His explicitly theological synthesis differs from methods that restrict historical study to narrower claims.
writings: The Theology of the Book of Revelation
Jude and the Relatives of Jesus in the Early Church
contributions: Renewed major scholarly debate about eyewitness testimony in Gospel formation
Advanced influential accounts of early divine Christology within Jewish monotheism
Expanded study of Jesus' relatives and the Jerusalem church
Integrated biblical theology with environmental ethics
scholars.influence: Highly influential in Gospel origins, early Christology, Revelation studies, historical Jesus research, and Christian theological readings of Scripture.
comparisons: With Craig Keener: both argue that the Gospels deserve serious historical treatment. Bauckham's distinctive emphasis is eyewitness testimony; Keener's is the density of cultural and documentary context.
With James Kugel and Jon Levenson: Bauckham draws heavily on early Jewish materials but develops Christian historical and christological conclusions from them.
With Emanuel Tov: Bauckham's historical synthesis depends on textual evidence whose manuscript forms and transmission fall within Tov's specialist domain.
scholars.who: A New Testament scholar and theologian best known for investigating whether the Gospels preserve identifiable eyewitness testimony.
scholars.whyHelpful: Bauckham helps readers examine how Gospel traditions may connect with named witnesses, the early Jerusalem community, and Jewish beliefs about the identity of Israel's God. He is useful when asking how early our Gospel information may be.

startWith.title: Jesus: A Very Short Introduction
startWith.reason: A concise and accessible introduction to his historical understanding of Yeshua.

startWith.title: Jesus and the Eyewitnesses
startWith.reason: His major, detailed argument about testimony and Gospel origins.

scholars.name: Jon D. Levenson
scholars.title: Albert A. List Professor of Jewish Studies, Harvard Divinity School
scholars.overview: A scholar of Hebrew Bible, Jewish interpretation, midrash, and Jewish-Christian relations whose work joins close literary reading with historical and theological analysis.
languages: His CV documents study of Modern Hebrew language and culture, and his field requires close work with Biblical Hebrew and Jewish interpretive texts. The reviewed sources do not provide a complete self-rated language inventory.
strengths: Close literary reading joined to Jewish theological interpretation
Resists treating historical criticism as the only legitimate context for meaning
Clarifies differences and shared themes between Judaism and Christianity
Brings biblical, Second Temple, rabbinic, medieval, and modern interpretation into conversation
limitations: His theological and canonical readings may not persuade scholars committed to strictly historical reconstruction.
His defense of particular Jewish readings can sharply challenge Christian universalizing interpretations.
Literary-theological synthesis does not replace text-critical work on variant manuscripts.
writings: Resurrection and the Restoration of Israel
The Death and Resurrection of the Beloved Son
Creation and the Persistence of Evil
Israel's Day of Light and Joy
contributions: Recovered resurrection as a significant theme within Israel's Scriptures and Jewish theology
Reframed sacrifice, beloved-son traditions, covenant, and divine love through close Jewish reading
Critiqued Christian supersessionist uses of Hebrew Scripture
Contributed sustained scholarship and dialogue on Jewish-Christian difference
scholars.influence: Influential in Hebrew Bible theology, Jewish studies, literary interpretation, resurrection studies, Sabbath research, and Jewish-Christian dialogue.
comparisons: With James Kugel: both emphasize the Bible's Jewish interpretive afterlives. Kugel often maps ancient interpretive assumptions; Levenson more directly develops literary and theological claims.
With Emanuel Tov: Levenson asks what texts mean within literary and theological contexts; Tov establishes the textual forms and transmission history that precede that work.

With Keener and Bauckham: Levenson shares interest in Second Temple interpretation but frequently challenges Christian readings that absorb Israel's particular identity into universal Christian categories.

sources.label: Harvard Divinity Bulletin interview on Sabbath

scholars.who: A Jewish scholar who reads the Hebrew Bible closely as literature and theology while tracing its interpretation through Jewish tradition.
scholars.whyHelpful: Levenson helps readers encounter Israel's Scriptures without treating Jewish meaning as merely a preface to Christianity. His work is especially valuable for covenant, sacrifice, resurrection, Sabbath, and Jewish-Christian differences.

startWith.title: Inheriting Abraham
startWith.reason: An accessible comparison of how Judaism, Christianity, and Islam understand Abraham.

startWith.title: Israel's Day of Light and Joy
startWith.reason: A focused study of the Sabbath's origin, development, and enduring Jewish meaning.
